channel.title: TradePose Research
channel.description: Quantitative research notes: backtests, statistics and strategy diagnostics

item.title: Intraday volatility follows a fixed cycle: should ATR be weighted by trading session?
item.description: Index volatility follows a fixed cycle within the day: largest at the US open, smallest in the Asian night. This post tests on NAS100 whether weighting the daily ATR by trading session brings the unit closer to the volatility the market actually shows. The answer depends on the horizon of the decision. Within a day, the weighted scale cuts the error of describing volatility by more than 30%; over multi-day holds the weights average back to 1 and the scale is the daily ATR. The post explains why, and how to compute the unit for intraday strategies.

item.title: Do popular indicator signals have an edge? 34 default-parameter signals on NAS100: path asymmetry and delayed limit orders, 2018–2025
item.description: The platform-default signals of the 17 most common technical-indicator families (moving-average crosses, MACD, RSI, Stochastic, CCI, Bollinger, Donchian, SuperTrend, Ichimoku, prior-day levels, opening range, round numbers), long and short, 34 in all, on 1-hour and 30-minute bars of Pepperstone NAS100 and FTMO US100: is the path after a signal asymmetric, do delayed limit orders around it earn anything, and how does holding each signal for 16 fifteen-minute bars compare with the market.

item.title: Shorting NAS100 at the open on option expiration day: the only one of 45 hypotheses that held
item.description: Two rounds of pre-registered structural-flow hypotheses on US index CFDs (45 in all: closing rebalancing, month end, FOMC, earnings nights, fixing times, rebalance days) left one signal standing at the family level: shorting NAS100 at 09:30 New York on monthly option expiration day for one hour, a window first found in an earlier scan of the same data and therefore labelled post hoc. This post records the base signal on Pepperstone NAS100 since 2018 and FTMO US100 since 2022, the delayed entry, the stop and the take profit that followed, the cost, the sizing, and the one read of 2026.

item.title: When a signal stays true, the engine enters once: how entry and exit signals are cleaned, and why scaling in is several strategies
item.description: The entry and exit conditions a strategy author hands to TradePose are booleans per bar, and they are often true for many bars in a row. The engine does not open a position on every bar. It cleans them into a strictly alternating sequence of entries and exits, so every position has one entry and one exit. This post explains the three cleaning stages, which signals are ignored, why the engine is built this way, and why scaling in or out should be written as several independent strategies combined in a portfolio.

item.title: Market benchmarks for 22 instruments: what simply holding earns by day, week and month
item.description: What does simply holding a market earn? Long and short day, week and month holds of 22 indexes, metals, commodities and currencies, with gaps inside every trade, as the benchmark to judge a strategy against.

item.title: Why the Sharpe ratio of a sparse strategy gets inflated: annualize over every trading day
item.description: A common way to compute a strategy's Sharpe ratio uses only the days with a closed trade and multiplies by the square root of 252. For a strategy that trades once a month, that overstates the Sharpe several times and ranks it above better strategies. This post shows where the error comes from, how TradePose builds the daily series instead, and how to fix it in your own code.

item.title: One entry opportunity, many exit policies: how the engine splits a strategy
item.description: TradePose splits every strategy into an entry opportunity and the trade policies applied to it. The opportunity is computed once, every policy runs on top of it in isolation, and each policy's trades line up one by one with the opportunities they came from, including the ones a delayed entry never filled. This post explains that split and why it makes layered research possible.

item.title: SuperTrend state trades: from 768 candidates to 1 strategy on watch (US100 and gold)
item.description: Following the strategy-selection methodology from 768 SuperTrend state candidates on US100 and gold, through calibration, the veto list, the entry and exit tree, leaf checks, combination and sizing, gave a 10-strategy portfolio: +USD 70,078 after cost in the selection period (2022-03 to 2025-12), max drawdown 4,723. Read once after the freeze, the validation period (2026-01 to 2026-10-23) lost USD 2,564. The state signal itself had no mean edge; the profit came mostly from exit parameters chosen on the same data. The portfolio is not deployed; the US100 4h held short in a bearish state (r14), still consistent in the validation period, is frozen as a new candidate and kept on watch.

item.title: How a backtest avoids look-ahead bias: bar timestamps, shift, and what happens inside one bar
item.description: A backtest can see the future in two quiet ways: by reading a bar's close before the bar has finished, and by assuming a convenient order of events inside a bar. This post explains when TradePose makes each decision, which part of avoiding look-ahead the engine guarantees and which part the strategy author owns, and the conservative rules it applies when one bar reaches several prices.

item.title: How to build 4-hour bars: daylight saving time makes backtests depend on their start date
item.description: The same 4-hour strategy on the same prices trades differently when the backtest starts in winter instead of summer. The usual resampling functions align only the first bar to the local clock and then add a fixed 4 hours per bar. This post explains how the problem appears, how to cut bars on the local wall clock, and how to win back the speed without giving up correctness.

item.title: MAE, G_MFE and profit factor: a quant research glossary
item.description: Terms and methods shared by our research and strategy reports: the calculation modes and volatility units and why they don't compare directly, MAE/G_MFE/MFE, performance and drawdown, the layer order, controls, favorable and adverse delayed entry, SL/TP and BE, how take profits and filters are judged, and the terms of the selection method.

item.title: Research map and method: how a strategy goes from a hypothesis to a frozen portfolio
item.description: The entry point to all our research: what a study declares before reading data, how the reading is calibrated against noise, the veto list for a base signal, the entry and exit layers, the final cost, correlation and sizing stage, the freeze, and the published studies in reading order.
